title: Yu Zhang 🐙🌘 (@yzhang_cs)
clean_title: Zero train–inference mismatch for linear attention in async RL
summary:
Zero Train–Inference Mismatch — now for linear attention, and under async RL 🎯
We got bitwise-exact trainer/generator parity for Gated DeltaNet (Qwen3.5-9B / 35B-A3B) on TorchTitan RL + vLLM, then asked the question nobody had actually tested in open source: does it help async RL?
Two firsts (as far as we know):
1️⃣ First open-source stack to hit train/inference logprob diff = 0 on a
linear-attention model
2️⃣ First to measure what zero mismatch is worth under async off-policy RL
How — smaller than it sounds:
• trainer and generator share one model definition (TorchTitan unified model). No more aligning trainer & generator op by op
• recurrent kernel everywhere on the forward (prefill + decode + trainer), chunked only for backward
• split-K off, batch-invariant GEMM, + a batch-invariant bmm for the MoE router
• we never touch FLA kernel internals — the recurrent kernel is intrinsically batch-invariant: one sequence's own state, fixed order, no cross-sequence reductions
• vLLM's linear-cache management + prefix caching keep working as-is
📊 Qwen3.5-9B + DAPO-Math, async at offpolicy = 4 / 12 / 32:
• logprob_diff = exactly 0 at step 0 ✅ every nonzero after that is staleness, not precision
• at offpolicy=32 the stock stack runs away past 0.065; ours holds ~0.035
• the unified model is free — the entire bill is the kernels
• also verified on MoE 35B-A3B and a 64-turn / 64K-context terminal agent
🤔 Now the honest part: it depends on the config. On math at offpolicy=12, BI leads on train reward and peaks highest on held-out AIME. On the terminal agent it's slightly ahead. On search, and on other math configs, the curves are indistinguishable. What is consistent is the numerics — BI keeps the gap from exploding as you widen the window. Cost: 2–3× trainer throughput (≈5× on the agent).
Our take: bitwise parity is a debugging tool, not a production default. Flip BI on for 20 on-policy steps — if the gap is 0 and your run is still broken, the infra is exonerated and the bug is in your data or your algorithm. That's worth 20 steps, not a whole run.
Next:
• make BI cheap (kill the 2–3×)
• more workloads, more seeds
• stay tuned for more complex agentic training recipes/tests 👀
Full writeup 🔗
We collaborated closely with the TorchTitan team, and we sincerely encourage everyone to check out TorchTitan RL. With its clean, efficient unified model architecture and native async RL design, we believe it is a strong foundation for your next RL engine.
#LLM #RL #agentic #pytorch #torchtitan
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HPENpSybEAAZM8-.jpg
clean_summary:
Zero train–inference mismatch is now achieved for linear attention models under asynchronous reinforcement learning. The work demonstrates that a shared model definition, recurrent kernels, and batch-invariant operations can produce bitwise-exact parity between training and inference log probabilities, even in async RL settings. Experiments with Qwen3.5-9B and DAPO-Math show that the logprob difference remains zero at step zero, with small staleness afterward, and the approach maintains stable numerics across different configurations.

The main insight is that this parity helps identify bugs in data or algorithms quickly, rather than being a default for production. Future work includes making bitwise parity cheaper, testing more workloads, and developing more complex agentic training recipes. The collaboration with TorchTitan highlights its efficiency and suitability as a foundation for RL engines.

title: Yu Zhang 🐙🌘 (@yzhang_cs)
clean_title: CAKE: Compiler-Agent Co-Design for Frontier Kernel Evolution
summary:
🍰 CAKE paper's out, the design bet: the compiler isn't a fixed black box the agent calls — it's part of the harness, and it's under evolution too.
CAKE didn't inherit existing abstraction layer. no tile/layout abstractions: the vocabulary was distilled by agents from a corpus of production kernels. every pattern the agent couldn't express pushed new primitives into the IR, and the analyses to keep them checkable. every barrier/layout bug that kept coming back became a verifier rule.
none of this can be designed up front. the IR has to co-evolve with the kernels, and the workload tells you what's missing, the corpus tells you if the fix broke anything.
the best language for an agent is the one that tells you what's illegal, what's slow, and which decision might made it faster.
Quoting @ye_combinator
🍰 another slice of CAKE just dropped: blackwell KDA kernels, ~2.05x geomean speedup vs FlashKDA:
by @avyyhuang
more cake kernels are baking 👀 not saying what CAKE actually is yet though, the full reveal is in the oven too.
clean_summary:
The CAKE paper introduces a new approach where the compiler is not a fixed black box called by the agent, but instead becomes part of the evolving system. The design avoids predefined abstraction layers, instead allowing the vocabulary to be distilled by agents from production kernels. When agents encounter patterns they can't express, they add new primitives to the intermediate representation (IR) and develop analysis tools to keep them checkable. The IR co-evolves with kernels based on workload feedback, and the workload indicates what's missing, while the corpus helps ensure fixes don't break existing functionality.

A key insight is that the best language for an agent is one that can identify what is illegal, slow, or could be optimized for speed. Recent progress includes a ~2.05x speedup using Blackwell KDA kernels compared to FlashKDA, with more kernel improvements in development. The full details and the underlying arXiv paper are available, along with related kernel backend updates.

title: Yu Zhang 🐙🌘 (@yzhang_cs)
summary:
🗒️✍️ specdec community moves fast
Quoting @vincentzed_cuda
DFlash2 beats dspark!
A lot of folks know about speculative decoding, but parallel drafting (like block diffusion) always had a fundamental dilemma:
To draft K tokens in 1 forward pass, you treat positions as conditionally independent. But language isn't conditionally independent; if token 2 changes, token 3 must change too!
If you use an autoregressive drafter, you pay K sequential forward passes. If you use independent diffusion drafting (DFlash 1), you get grammar breaks and low acceptance rates. Recent methods like DSpark try to patch this with a sequential Markov head, but the backbone stays non-causal and you have to project across the full ~150k vocab at every step.
DFlash (2!) fixes this in a really elegant way without adding extra forward passes:
1. grouped dynamic conv
Unlike DSpark where the backbone is purely parallel, here each hidden state projects a causal 1D filter (base kernel + dynamic input projection per channel group) before attention and MLP. This propagates local sequential context across the draft block before full attention step.
2. transition code book in low rank space Instead of DSpark's full-vocab sequential loop or taking independent argmax: • filter down to top-k candidate tokens per position from unary logits. • learned two low-rank codebooks (E_pred, E_succ) of rank r. • use dynamic beam along the block:
Score(xₜ | xₜ₋₁) = Logit(xₜ) + ⟨ E_pred(xₜ₋₁) ⊙ W hₜ, E_succ(xₜ) ⟩
This way transition scoring is just small dot products over the top-k candidates, you recover autoregressive sequence coherence in microseconds—beating DSpark by +25% on acceptance length (5.46 vs 4.36 on Qwen3.8) and getting 3.43× speedup at single-pass latency!
